title: Hunger and thirst get a share
hookLine: once the gods have moved in, two more voices speak up: hunger and thirst want a home too
tomorrow: the self enters through the crown of the head
last: THE BODY IS A HOME FOR THE GODS.

lines: HUNGER AND THIRST: WHAT ABOUT US?
cards: Everyone's moved in. Fire has the mouth, the sun has the eyes, the moon has the heart. The house is full and humming.
Then there's a knock. Two figures stand outside, and they were there before the gods arrived. In fact, they're why the gods went house-hunting at all.
Their names are hunger and thirst, ashanaya and pipasa, and they say to the self: what about us? Find us a place too. You know these two: mid-afternoon, midnight at the fridge, long meetings.
The Aitareya gives them a whole verse.

teach.h: HUNGER AND THIRST WERE THERE FIRST.
teach.b: Here's the order in the story. When the gods first fell into the great ocean, the self touched that whole creation with hunger and thirst. That's why the gods asked for a home: they wanted a place to eat.
So hunger and thirst are older than the house. They didn't break in. They were part of the plan.
Now, with the gods settled, the two ask: find a place for us. The self doesn't banish them, or scold them as enemies of the spirit. It says, more or less: I'll give you a share among these gods.

teach.h: A SHARE IN EVERY GOD'S OFFERING.
teach.b: That's why, the text explains, whenever an offering is made to any god, hunger and thirst share in it. Nobody is shamed for being hungry.
One way to hear this story is beside a teaching that runs all through Hindu tradition.

teach.h: KAMA: ONE OF FOUR AIMS OF LIFE.
teach.b: Kama, desire, pleasure, love, is counted as one of the four aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, right living; artha, making a living; kama, enjoyment; and moksha, freedom. Wanting isn't treated as the enemy.

teach.h: INSIDE DHARMA, NOT IN PLACE OF IT.
teach.b: But notice where the seat is in the story: inside the offering, beside the gods, not in place of them.
The tradition holds kama the same way, inside dharma. Enjoy the meal, the song, the love, and enjoy them rightly. So when a craving shows up, the question isn't how to kill it.
It's whether it's sitting at the table, or trying to run the house.

how: Teachers of the Aitareya read this passage when explaining why appetite goes with every sense, and in Vedic ritual each offering is made to a particular deity, the share the passage says hunger and thirst join.

o: the fire god's hunger, living in the mouth
hunger and thirst, sharing in every offering

games.q: hunger, thirst and the gods — tap the pairs.
p: find a place for us too

s: the self banishes hunger and thirst from the body
it gives them a share among the gods instead.
the gods asked for a home because they were hungry
the self had touched creation with hunger and thirst; the gods wanted a place to eat.
Hindu tradition counts desire among the four aims of life
kama sits with dharma, artha and moksha: wanting has a place, inside dharma.

games.q: Nani is keeping a fast, and still cooks your favorite dinner and tells you to enjoy it. so is wanting food bad, or not?
o: it's bad: real devotion kills every desire.
not bad: kama is one of life's four aims, held inside dharma.
only on fast days; on other days anything goes.
games.why: the self gave hunger and thirst a share among the gods instead of banishing them. Hindu tradition keeps kama as an aim of life, inside dharma: a fast steers wanting, it doesn't condemn it.

practice: Check gently for hunger, thirst, or some other wanting: for your phone, for news, for this to be over. Don't obey it and don't fight it; just find where it lives in the body, the stomach, the throat, the hands.
Let it sit there, known and given room, without running the house.

wordCard.voice: Appetite, the hunger and thirst that ask the self for a place. In the Aitareya, they're given no room of their own, but a share in whatever is offered to every god. Its big sister is kama, desire, one of the four aims of life.

orig.note: Sanskrit aśanāyā-pipāse: hunger (aśanāyā) and thirst (pipāsā), a pair in Aitareya 1.2.

carryVoice: Take this with you: kama, wanting has its place. In this story, even hunger gets a seat at the gods' table. See you tomorrow.
